claims.text: The target alloy has composition Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 and is produced by additive manufacturing.
The starting alloy has an FCC matrix.
Al, Co, Cr, Fe, Ni, and Ti are uniformly distributed in the starting alloy.
The starting alloy contains minimal secondary-phase precipitation.
Degradation of the alloy is governed by selective oxidation of Cr and Ti.
In oxidizing environments, Cr and Ti preferentially form a continuous mixed Cr2O3/TiO2 surface scale.
A continuous mixed Cr2O3/TiO2 scale retards oxygen ingress and preserves mechanical integrity.
Under low-oxygen reducing conditions, insufficient external scale formation permits internal oxygen penetration.
Internal oxidation produces discrete oxide precipitates, particularly along grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary oxide precipitates act as initiation sites for localized microcracking and cyclic degradation.
Oxide morphology, continuity, and surface-versus-grain-boundary distribution mediate oxidation-induced microstructural damage.
Air-exposed specimens will form a uniform protective scale with minimal internal oxidation.
Air-exposed specimens will retain strength and fatigue performance relative to the unexposed baseline.
Low-oxygen nitrogen exposure will cause internal grain-boundary oxidation, reduced fatigue performance, and localized microcracking.
The proposed regime applies over 800–1000 °C for exposure durations up to 120 hours.
Identical specimens should be compared after exposure in air and in nitrogen with low oxygen at 900 °C for 120 hours.
The hypothesis is falsified if both environments produce similar oxide-scale characteristics, internal-oxidation profiles, and no significant mechanical-performance differences from baseline.
